title: Twilight means “two-light”
body: The word comes from the Old English twi- (the same “two/half” root in twin and twice) joined to light — the half-light that is neither true day nor true night. Its German cousin Zwielicht carries exactly the same idea. So every time you say “twilight,” you’re literally naming the in-between light.

title: Why one phase is called “nautical”
body: Nautical twilight (sun 6°–12° below the horizon) is named for sailors. It is the only stretch of the evening when the sea horizon is still faintly visible AND the navigational stars have come out — the exact conditions a navigator needs to bring a star down to the horizon with a sextant. Miss that window and you wait until dawn.

title: The Belt of Venus and Earth’s own shadow
body: Look east just after sunset on a clear evening and you’ll often see a soft pink band hugging the horizon — the Belt of Venus, sunlight reddened by the atmosphere and backscattered toward you. Below it sits a dusky blue-grey arc: that is the literal shadow of the Earth, cast onto its own air, rising as the sun sinks.

title: Twilight is shortest at the equator
body: Near the equator the sun drops almost straight down, so it crosses the twilight angles quickly — dusk can be over in about 20 minutes. Toward the poles the sun grazes the horizon at a shallow angle and twilight stretches for hours. Far enough north or south in summer, it never finishes at all.

title: The green flash is real
body: For a second or two as the last sliver of sun disappears, its top edge can flare emerald green. The atmosphere acts like a weak prism, bending green light slightly higher than red, while a near-horizon mirage magnifies the effect. It’s genuinely fleeting and genuinely prized — Jules Verne built a whole novel around chasing it.

title: “Between dog and wolf”
body: French has a beautiful name for dusk: entre chien et loup — “between dog and wolf” — the moment so dim you can’t tell the familiar dog from the dangerous wolf. Scots gives us the gloaming, and many cultures keep a special word for this uncertain, shape-shifting light.

title: Blue hour vs golden hour
body: Photographers prize two slices of twilight. Golden hour is the low-sun period just before sunset, all long shadows and warm light. Blue hour follows once the sun is down — roughly civil twilight — when the sky takes on a deep, even blue and city lights balance the fading sky. Blue hour is short, which is why photographers move fast.

title: Sunsets are blue on Mars
body: On Mars the daytime sky is butterscotch, but around sunset the glow near the sun turns blue — the reverse of Earth. Fine airborne dust scatters red light away and lets blue wavelengths linger close to the sun. NASA’s rovers have photographed these eerie blue Martian twilights directly.

title: Why 18° marks the edge of night
body: Astronomical twilight ends when the sun sits 18° below the horizon. Below that angle, scattered sunlight in the upper atmosphere no longer brightens the sky in any way a telescope can detect — the background goes as dark as it will get. That threshold is why deep-sky observers wait for “astronomical dark.”

title: The sun you watch set has already set
body: Atmospheric refraction lifts the sun’s image by roughly half a degree near the horizon — about its own width. So at the instant you see the lower edge touch the sea, the sun is geometrically already below the true horizon. That’s why sunrise and sunset are reckoned at −0.833°, not 0°.

title: Where −0.833° actually comes from
body: That oddly precise sunset angle is two effects added together: about 34 arc-minutes of atmospheric refraction lifting the sun’s image, plus roughly 16 arc-minutes for the sun’s own radius (we call it “set” when the upper edge, not the centre, drops). Fifty arc-minutes total — five-sixths of a degree.

title: The false dawn
body: After astronomical twilight fully ends, a faint cone of light can still lean up from the horizon along the path of the planets — the zodiacal light, sunlight scattered off dust drifting in the plane of the solar system. Before sunrise it has been called the “false dawn,” fooling early risers for centuries.

title: The counterglow you almost never see
body: Fainter even than the zodiacal light is the Gegenschein, or counterglow — a dim oval of light sitting exactly opposite the sun in a fully dark sky. It’s sunlight backscattered straight off interplanetary dust grains, and from light-polluted ground it’s essentially invisible; you need a moonless, twilight-free night far from any city.

title: St. Petersburg’s White Nights
body: Around 60° north — St. Petersburg, Stockholm, Helsinki — the midsummer sun dips so shallowly that the sky never passes beyond civil or nautical twilight. The result is weeks of luminous “white nights,” celebrated with festivals, all-night strolls and a famous run of cultural events.

title: Alpenglow after the sun is gone
body: Minutes after sunset, high peaks can blush pink or orange even though the valley below is already dark. This alpenglow is indirect sunlight — reddened by its long passage through the atmosphere — bouncing off particles and snow onto the summits. It also appears, fainter, before sunrise.

title: Crepuscular rays fan from the dusk
body: Those dramatic sunbeams that spread from behind a cloud take their name straight from twilight: crepuscular, from the Latin crepusculum, “dusk.” Stranger still are anticrepuscular rays, which appear to converge again at the point exactly opposite the sun — an illusion of perspective on parallel beams.

title: Creatures of the twilight
body: Animals most active at dawn and dusk are called crepuscular — deer, rabbits, many bats and moths, and house cats. The dim light is a survival compromise: bright enough to see by, but dark enough to hide from predators that rule full daylight or the dead of night.

title: Bats clock in at dusk
body: Most insect-eating bats emerge right around civil-to-nautical twilight, and it’s no accident — the gnats and midges they hunt swarm in the same fading light. Leaving too early risks being picked off by day-hunting hawks; leaving too late means missing the insect rush. Dusk is the sweet spot.

title: Flowers that wait for the dark
body: Vespertine plants — moonflower, evening primrose, night-blooming jasmine — keep their petals shut all day and open only at twilight. They’re courting night-flying moths, advertising with pale colours that stay visible in low light and scents that strengthen after sunset, when their daytime competitors have closed up shop.

title: Dusk and dawn are mirror images
body: The evening sequence — sunset, then civil, nautical and astronomical dusk — runs in exact reverse at dawn. The sun retraces the same depression angles in the opposite order, which is why almanacs list “nautical dawn” and “nautical dusk” as matching bookends around the night.

title: Twilight is longest at the solstices
body: At mid-latitudes, evening twilight lasts longest around the summer and winter solstices and is shortest near the equinoxes. The reason is geometry: near the equinoxes the sun plunges almost straight down through the twilight angles, but near the solstices it slides down at a shallow slant, taking far longer to fall the same 18°.

title: Twilight written into the rules
body: Plenty of laws hinge on civil twilight. “Lighting-up time,” when vehicles must show lights, hunting hours, and even when certain crimes count as “nighttime” offences are often defined as a set number of minutes after sunset — landing squarely in civil twilight, the point where useful outdoor light finally gives out.

title: First light, last light
body: Armed forces plan around two twilight moments: BMNT (Begin Morning Nautical Twilight) and EENT (End Evening Nautical Twilight). They mark when there’s just enough light to move and aim, or just enough dark to hide — which is exactly why dawn nautical twilight has been the classic hour for attacks and amphibious landings.

title: The dawn chorus rides the twilight
body: Songbirds sing most furiously in the half-hour around dawn, peaking in civil twilight before the sun is up. The pre-dawn air is calm and sound carries far, it’s too dim to forage efficiently, and a loud morning song signals to rivals and mates that a bird survived the night in fine voice.

title: Mercury, the twilight planet
body: Mercury never wanders far from the sun, so you can only catch it low in bright twilight, just after sunset or before sunrise. It’s so elusive that, by legend, Copernicus complained on his deathbed that he’d never once managed to see it — defeated by the murky air near the horizon.

title: The evening star and the morning star
body: Venus blazes in twilight as either the “evening star” or the “morning star,” never both at once. The ancient Greeks thought they were two different objects — Hesperus at dusk, Phosphorus at dawn — until they realised it was the same brilliant planet swinging from one side of the sun to the other.

title: Earthshine — the old moon in the new moon’s arms
body: On a thin crescent at twilight, you can often make out the rest of the moon’s disc glowing faintly grey. That’s earthshine: sunlight bouncing off Earth, onto the moon, and back to your eye. Leonardo da Vinci was the first to explain it correctly, centuries before anyone left the planet to confirm it.

title: The moon has no twilight
body: With essentially no atmosphere, the moon has nothing to scatter sunlight, so its day-night line is a knife-edge — full glare on one side, black sky and stars on the other. Yet Apollo astronauts reported a faint glow along the lunar horizon at “sunset,” a lingering mystery often pinned on electrically levitated dust.

title: Ozone helps paint the twilight blue
body: The deep blue overhead at dusk isn’t only Rayleigh scattering. High up, ozone absorbs red and yellow light through its Chappuis bands, and at twilight sunlight takes a very long, ozone-rich path through the atmosphere — stripping out the warm tones and leaving the cool, saturated blue we see after sunset.

title: When volcanoes stain the dusk purple
body: After major eruptions like Krakatoa in 1883, twilights around the world turned an unearthly purple and crimson for months. Fine volcanic aerosols flung into the stratosphere scatter light at high altitude, adding a glowing “purple light” above the normal twilight — vivid skies that some link to the lurid backdrop of Munch’s “The Scream.”

title: A goddess’s girdle
body: The rosy Belt of Venus borrows its name from the cestus — the magical girdle of the goddess Venus (Aphrodite), said to make its wearer irresistible. Astronomers liked the image of a glowing pink band wrapped around the horizon, and the poetic name stuck to a perfectly ordinary trick of scattered light.

title: “Red sky at night, sailor’s delight”
body: The old rhyme has real physics behind it. In mid-latitudes weather generally moves west to east, so a glowing red sunset means the western sky is clear and dusty with high pressure — fair weather inbound. A red sunrise suggests that clear, dry air has already passed to the east, with wetter weather following.

title: Owl-light and cockshut
body: English once had richer words for dusk. “Owl-light” was the dim hour when owls take wing, and “cockshut” (used by Shakespeare) named the evening twilight — the time to shut up the poultry for the night. Both have faded from use, leaving us with the plainer “dusk” and “gloaming.”

title: L’heure bleue, bottled
body: The French call blue hour l’heure bleue — and in 1912 the perfumer Jacques Guerlain bottled the idea, naming a fragrance after “the hour when the sun has set and the night has not yet found its star.” The notion that twilight has its own mood and scent is old, and surprisingly literal.

title: Pillars of light at the horizon
body: On cold, calm twilights, vertical shafts of light can rise above the sinking sun or distant lamps — light pillars. They’re not beams but reflections: countless flat, plate-like ice crystals drifting nearly horizontal in the cold air, each bouncing light toward you, stacking into a glowing column.

title: Sixteen sunsets a day
body: Astronauts aboard the International Space Station orbit Earth roughly every 90 minutes, which means they race through about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every single day. Each orbital twilight flashes past in seconds — a thin, brilliant arc of blue and orange wrapping the limb of the planet below.

title: Aviators get their own twilight
body: Pilots care about more than ground twilight, because at altitude the geometry shifts: from a cruising jet the sun can still be up while the ground below is already dark, stretching the usable light. Flight rules define night relative to the end of evening civil twilight, the moment terrestrial reference truly gives out.

title: The hour your eyes switch over
body: Twilight is when your vision changes hardware. As light fades, the colour-sensing cones in your eye hand off to the more sensitive rods — a transition called the Purkinje shift. Reds fade to near-black while blues and greens hang on, which is why a red flower and green leaves can look equally bright at noon yet utterly different at dusk.

title: Why dusk often out-reds dawn
body: Evening skies frequently glow redder than morning ones. Through the day, the sun heats the ground and stirs up dust, pollen and pollution, thickening the low-altitude haze that reddens light near the horizon. By dawn the air has often settled and cleaned overnight, so sunrises can look cooler and clearer than the sunsets that preceded them.

title: The deep-sky observer’s green light
body: Serious astronomers don’t just wait for sunset — they wait for the end of astronomical twilight, when the last skyglow drains away and faint galaxies and nebulae finally lift out of the background. Depending on your latitude and season, that fully dark window can be generous in winter and frustratingly brief, or absent, in high-latitude summer.

title: Earth’s shadow climbs at a steady pace
body: The dusky band of Earth’s shadow in the eastern sky doesn’t just sit there — it rises as the sun sets, climbing at the same rate the sun descends, very roughly a degree every four minutes. Watch the pink Belt of Venus above it lift and fade, and you’re literally watching the planet’s own shadow sweep up the sky.

title: Volcanoes in Turner’s sunsets
body: In 2007 a team of atmospheric scientists measured the balance of red and green in the skies of hundreds of paintings made between 1500 and 1900. Sunsets painted in the years after big eruptions came out measurably redder. Turner’s blazing skies from after the 1815 eruption of Tambora are among the clearest examples: he was painting what the aerosols were doing to real sunsets.

title: The night Krakatoa darkened the world
body: When Krakatoa erupted in August 1883, the blast threw megatons of fine ash into the stratosphere. For the next two years, sunsets across the globe blazed in colours never seen before — vivid crimsons, greens and purples that lasted hours after the sun had set. Reports poured in from London to Honolulu of skies looking like vast fires.

title: The brightest stars come out in nautical twilight
body: The brightest stars — Sirius, Arcturus, Vega, Capella — appear while the Sun is 6° to 12° down, in nautical twilight; fainter ones wait for astronomical twilight or full dark. Ancient calendars leaned on this: in Egypt, the first sighting of Sirius low in the dawn twilight, its heliacal rising, announced the season of the Nile flood.

title: Sunset as a sacred boundary
body: Many traditions start the day at sunset rather than midnight. The Jewish Sabbath begins at sunset on Friday and ends on Saturday at nightfall, traditionally when three medium stars can be seen, which falls in nautical twilight. Islamic prayer times are tied to the Sun too: Maghrib just after sunset, and Isha once the red glow of twilight has gone.

title: Measuring the air from the length of twilight
body: In the 11th century the Andalusian scholar Ibn Muʿādh reasoned that twilight lasts until the Sun is about 19° below the horizon, and that the last glow must be sunlight reaching the top of the atmosphere. From that angle he estimated the air to be about 52 miles deep — one of the first attempts to measure the height of the atmosphere.

title: The three-star fix
body: A navigator’s favourite moment is the end of nautical twilight, when the bright stars are out and the sea horizon is still sharp. Three stars chosen roughly 120° apart give three position lines; they rarely meet in a point but form a small triangle, the “cocked hat,” with the ship inside it. Too dark and the horizon vanishes; too light and the stars do.

title: The grunion run by moonlight
body: California grunion — small silvery fish — ride the highest tides of spring and summer onto beaches at night to spawn, almost always within the hour after high tide under a full or new moon. Their timing is so precise it can be predicted months in advance, and people gather at dusk to watch them pour ashore.

title: Shadow bands before an eclipse
body: In the minute or two before and after totality in a solar eclipse, faint ripples of light and shade can race across white ground — shadow bands. The last thin sliver of Sun shines through turbulent air near the ground and in the lower atmosphere, which breaks its light into moving stripes. It is the same turbulence that makes stars twinkle.

title: The afterglow is not the last light
body: Roughly 15 to 30 minutes after a vivid sunset, a second, softer glow can light up the western sky — the afterglow or secondary twilight arch. It comes from sunlight scattered off the high stratosphere, well above the coloured layer of the primary sunset, arriving at a slightly different angle. Pristine skies show it best.

title: Sunrise seen from orbit is blue-rimmed
body: Astronauts looking toward a rising sun from the ISS see its disc appear through a thin, brilliant blue arc — the Earth’s atmosphere glowing in refracted sunlight. That thin shell of blue is all the air there is. It looks frighteningly narrow from 400 kilometres up, just a hair of colour between the blackness and the planet.

title: Northern words for dusk
body: Languages of the far north are rich in words for dim light. Swedish has skymning for dusk and gryning for dawn; Finnish calls twilight hämärä; Norwegians speak of blåtimen, the blue hour, in the long winter afternoons when the Sun barely rises and the snow and sky glow blue.

title: The glow that follows the Sun
body: After sunset the brightest part of the sky is the glow above where the Sun went down, and it moves as the Sun moves below the horizon. At high latitudes in midsummer you can watch it creep along the northern horizon through the night, from the north-west at dusk to the north-east before dawn, never quite fading.

title: Stonehenge and the solstice sunrise
body: Stonehenge’s axis aligns almost exactly with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. The builders didn’t need clocks — they watched the horizon and tracked where twilight first broke along the skyline. Monuments aligned to sunrise or sunset appear on every inhabited continent, suggesting ancient peoples were keenly aware of the sun’s daily and annual arc.

title: Jupiter at dusk is often mistaken for a UFO
body: Jupiter can blaze so brightly in evening twilight that it regularly draws UFO reports — it outshines every star, doesn’t twinkle like one, and moves slowly enough to seem stationary. It’s often the first point of light to appear after sunset, hanging in the brightening west like a misplaced aircraft landing light that refuses to move.

title: Look slightly away to see more
body: The centre of your eye’s retina is packed with colour-sensing cones and has almost no rods, the cells that work in dim light. So in the dark, a faint star can vanish when you stare straight at it and reappear when you look a little to one side. Astronomers call this averted vision and use it deliberately.

title: Fairies at the threshold
body: In many European folk traditions, twilight was a dangerous threshold — a time when the veil between worlds thinned and fairies, spirits or the dead could cross over. This liminal logic appears in Celtic lore, Scandinavian beliefs and in countless cautionary tales: don’t travel at dusk, don’t name things by twilight, don’t stray from the path when you can’t see the road ahead.

title: Debussy’s clouds
body: Debussy’s orchestral Nocturnes (1899) open with “Nuages,” which he described as “the unchanging aspect of the sky, with the slow and solemn motion of the clouds, fading away in grey tones lightly tinged with white.” Like the Impressionist painters he admired, he was after the feel of light and air rather than a story.

title: Noctilucent clouds glow after all other clouds go dark
body: Ordinary clouds are lit from above and go dark at sunset. But noctilucent clouds — thin wisps of ice forming 80 km up, at the edge of space — are so high that the sun still shines on them long after the lower sky has gone black. Silvery-blue and electric, they’re visible in summer twilight at high latitudes, drifting in patterns no weather cloud makes.

title: Keats and the rosy stubble fields
body: Keats wrote “To Autumn” in September 1819 after an evening walk near Winchester, telling a friend that “a stubble plain looks warm — in the same way that some pictures look warm.” The poem ends at dusk: “while barred clouds bloom the soft-dying day, / And touch the stubble-plains with rosy hue.”

title: How long is the shortest possible twilight?
body: At the equator on the equinox, the sun plunges nearly perpendicular to the horizon, and civil twilight lasts only about 20–24 minutes. At a latitude of 50° at the same season it stretches to around 35 minutes. Near the poles in winter, the sun may linger at −6° for hours, keeping civil twilight alive long after a brief, low-slung noon.

title: Saturn’s ring-shadow at dusk
body: Through even a small telescope at dusk, Saturn’s rings cast a visible shadow onto the planet’s cloud tops. The shadow’s angle shifts year by year as Saturn’s 29-year orbit changes our viewing perspective. When the rings are tilted edge-on to us — roughly every 15 years — they nearly vanish, and Saturn looks oddly plain and alone.

title: Polynesian star paths
body: Polynesian navigators memorised ‘star paths’ — the rising and setting points of specific stars on the horizon, all of which occur in twilight when sky and sea horizon are both visible. They could also read the stars’ zenith points: a star that passes directly overhead indicates your latitude. They crossed the Pacific without instruments, using the twilight sky as a chart.

title: The dip of the sea horizon
body: From above the water the sea horizon lies slightly below true level, because the Earth curves away. The dip is about 1.76 arc-minutes times the square root of your eye height in metres: roughly 5′ from a 9-metre deck. Navigators subtract it from every sextant altitude, or the fix drifts by that many nautical miles.

title: Reef fish synchronise their spawning to the moon and dusk
body: Many coral reef fish release eggs and sperm at the exact moment of dusk, in the days just after the full moon. The falling light signals evening, the moon cycle syncs the cohort, and the timing disperses eggs into the ocean as night falls — when visual predators are handicapped. The whole reef population co-ordinates with the sky.

title: The sky in “The Scream”
body: Munch wrote that the idea for “The Scream” came on an evening walk when “the sky suddenly turned blood red.” Scientists have offered two explanations: the vivid twilights that followed Krakatoa in 1883–84, which Norway saw too, or nacreous “mother-of-pearl” clouds, which glow in wavy bands over Oslo on some winter evenings. Nobody can be sure which he saw.

title: Leaves close their pores at dusk
body: Leaves take in carbon dioxide through tiny pores called stomata, which open in daylight so photosynthesis can run. As the light fades in the evening most plants close them, saving water they would otherwise lose overnight. Light is one of the main signals, so falling light at dusk helps tell the leaves the day’s work is over.

title: The shadow of the Moon during an eclipse
body: During a total solar eclipse, the Moon’s umbra sweeps across Earth at roughly 1,700 km/h — faster than a jet. Observers in the shadow’s path watch the sky darken in minutes, not hours, and full ‘eclipse twilight’ descends: planets and bright stars appear, the horizon glows 360° as if at dusk, and the temperature drops. Then the shadow races on and day snaps back.

title: Ra’s journey through the night
body: In Egyptian belief the setting Sun was Ra entering the Duat, the underworld, to travel through the twelve hours of the night before being reborn at dawn. Tomb texts such as the Amduat map that voyage hour by hour, and the dead hoped to join Ra’s boat and rise with him in the morning.

title: West windows and the evening sun
body: Most medieval churches were built with the altar at the east end, which puts the great west window or rose where the low afternoon and evening sun strikes it. Stained glass is lit from outside, so these windows come alive late in the day, throwing coloured light down the length of the nave just as the Sun sinks.

title: Mother-of-pearl clouds
body: In the depths of a high-latitude winter, thin clouds can form 15 to 25 km up in the frigid stratosphere. Lit by the Sun from below the horizon, these nacreous clouds shine in vivid pastel pinks, greens and blues, like the inside of a shell, and they stay bright well after sunset and before sunrise, when ordinary clouds have gone grey.

title: The evening rise of melatonin
body: Your body starts releasing melatonin, the hormone that prepares you for sleep, in the evening as the light fades — typically a couple of hours before your usual bedtime. Bright light, and blue-rich light especially, holds it back. That is why a bright screen late at night can delay the signal that night has arrived.

title: Stars don’t twinkle — air does
body: Stars appear to twinkle at the horizon during twilight because their light travels through a long, turbulent wedge of atmosphere before reaching your eye. The star itself is perfectly steady; pockets of air at different temperatures bend and deflect the light erratically. Planets twinkle far less because their discs are wide enough to average out the turbulence.

title: Eos, goddess of the dawn
body: In Greek mythology, Eos was the goddess of the dawn, tasked with opening the gates of heaven each morning so her brother Helios could drive his chariot of the sun across the sky. Her rosy fingers — rhododactylos — tinted the early sky, and Homer invokes her in the Iliad and Odyssey more than a dozen times. She is, essentially, a deity of twilight.

title: The polar explorer’s endless twilight
body: In the high Arctic or Antarctic in summer, the sun circles the sky at low angles for weeks, never rising high and never setting. Explorers describe the disorienting, perpetual twilight quality of polar summer midnights — the sun neither up nor down, casting sideways shadows that don’t move the way shadows should, the sky a uniform pale gold.

title: Bracketing through the blue hour
body: The light changes steadily through twilight: around the end of civil twilight the sky dims by about a stop every few minutes. Photographers bracket their exposures — the same frame shot darker and brighter — and keep shooting as the balance between the fading sky and the brightening city lights slides past its best moment.

title: Sunset light left the Sun eight minutes ago
body: The sunlight lighting your sunset left the Sun about 8 minutes 20 seconds earlier, after crossing roughly 150 million kilometres of nearly empty space. All the colour happens in the last few hundred kilometres, as it slants through the atmosphere and loses its blue to scattering.

title: Sibelius’s midsummer nights
body: From 1904 Jean Sibelius lived and composed at Ainola, a house by Lake Tuusula north of Helsinki, at about 60° north. At midsummer the Sun there sinks only about 6° below the horizon at midnight, so the night barely passes the end of civil twilight — the pale, sleepless June light that is part of Finnish life.

title: Fireflies start at dusk
body: Many North American fireflies start their courtship flashing in the dusk, soon after sunset. In the common eastern firefly, the males fly low and flash a J-shaped streak of light, and females in the grass answer after a set delay; each species has its own code of flashes and pauses. The displays thin out as full darkness comes.

title: Aperitivo hour
body: In Italy the aperitivo, a light drink with small bites before dinner, fills the early evening. The custom is often traced to Turin, where vermouth was first sold commercially in the late 1700s, and it now belongs to the hour when work ends and the light goes golden over the piazza.

title: Bioluminescent waves glow at night
body: On certain warm coasts, breaking waves glow blue-green at night — not phosphorescence but bioluminescence from marine dinoflagellates called Noctiluca scintillans. As dusk falls and the sea darkens, each crashing wave disturbs millions of single-celled organisms that flash blue as a stress response. Twilight swimmers describe an uncanny experience of leaving a glowing wake.

title: The zodiacal band circles the whole sky
body: The zodiacal light — usually seen as a cone after dusk or before dawn — is actually one section of a complete band of scattered light encircling the entire sky along the ecliptic. In perfectly dark conditions far from any city, you can trace this zodiacal band all the way across the sky, connected to the Gegenschein on the opposite side. Most people never see it at all.

title: Stand-to at dawn and dusk
body: Armies long treated dawn and dusk as the most dangerous times of day, when an attacker could move in poor light. In the trenches of the First World War both sides held “stand-to” twice a day, every soldier armed and on the fire step through morning and evening twilight, until the light was full or fully gone.

title: Autumn mornings for the zodiacal light
body: The faint cone of zodiacal light rises along the path of the planets. It is easiest to see when that path stands steeply from the horizon: for northern observers, in the east before dawn in September and October, and in the west after dusk in February to April. Southern-hemisphere seasons are the reverse.

title: Skylight is polarised
body: Skylight is polarised, and most strongly in a band about 90° away from the Sun. Polarising sunglasses or a camera filter darken that band dramatically. Bees and many other insects can see this pattern and use it as a compass even when the Sun itself is hidden.

title: The Angelus bell
body: In Catholic tradition the Angelus bell rings three times a day — morning, noon and evening — calling people to pause for a short prayer. Millet’s painting “The Angelus” (1857–59) shows two farm workers stopping in a potato field at the evening bell, heads bowed against a glowing sky.

title: Rayleigh scattering explains every blue sky and red sunset
body: Gas molecules scatter short-wavelength (blue) light far more than long-wavelength (red) light — the relationship goes with the fourth power of frequency, meaning blue scatters roughly ten times more than red. At noon the sky is blue because you’re looking away from the sun. At sunset you’re looking through a thick slab of atmosphere toward the sun, and all the blue has already been scattered away, leaving red.

title: Lunar distances in the twilight
body: Before reliable chronometers, navigators found longitude by measuring the angle between the Moon and a bright star or planet, often in twilight when both the sky objects and the horizon could be seen. The working took hours by hand, and an error of one minute of arc in that angle could put a ship about 30 nautical miles off. Harrison’s marine chronometers gradually made the method unnecessary.

title: Retreat, then Taps
body: On American military bases the day closes in two calls. At the end of the duty day, often near sunset, “Retreat” sounds and the flag comes down. Later, at lights out, a bugler plays “Taps,” the 24-note call written in 1862 during the Civil War, which is also played at military funerals.

title: Robins singing into the night
body: European robins are among the last birds to fall silent at dusk and the first to sing at dawn. In towns they often keep singing long after dark, under streetlights; studies suggest urban robins shift to night singing partly to escape daytime traffic noise.

title: The ‘Ashen Light’ of Venus
body: In the 17th century, Giovanni Battista Riccioli reported seeing a faint glow on the dark side of Venus’s crescent at twilight — the ‘Ashen Light’. Unlike earthshine on the moon, this can’t be reflected earthlight. Its cause remains debated: atmospheric lightning, airglow, or just optical illusion. Observers have reported it for nearly 400 years, and it’s never been definitively explained.

title: Why fog forms on clear, calm nights
body: Radiation fog is made overnight. On a clear, still evening the ground loses the day’s heat to the sky, the air touching it cools to its dew point, and mist begins to gather in low spots, often thickening towards dawn. Cloud cover stops it by acting as a blanket, and wind stops it by stirring the cold layer away.

title: Twilight in the sea — the mesopelagic zone
body: The ocean has its own twilight zone: the mesopelagic layer, 200 to 1,000 metres down, where sunlight fades to near-zero. Creatures there live in perpetual dim blue light, making the largest daily migration on Earth — rising toward the surface at dusk and sinking at dawn. The biomass involved is staggering, and the carbon they transport downward is a crucial part of the ocean’s carbon cycle.

title: The blue flash
body: Sometimes the last sliver of the setting Sun turns blue or violet instead of green. The same bending of light that makes the green flash separates blue even further, but blue is so heavily scattered on its way through the low atmosphere that it usually never reaches you. It takes exceptionally clean, clear air, which makes a blue flash much rarer than a green one.

title: The Egyptian night of twelve hours
body: Ancient Egyptians divided the night into twelve hours, marked by groups of stars called decans rising in turn. Star tables painted inside coffin lids listed which decan marked each hour through the year. Because the night itself grows and shrinks with the seasons, these hours were longer in winter than in summer.

title: Twilight of the gods
body: Norse myth calls the end of the world Ragnarök, “the fate of the gods.” A variant form, ragnarøkkr, used by Snorri Sturluson in the 13th century, means “the twilight of the gods,” and that version was rendered in German as Götterdämmerung — the title Wagner gave the last opera of his Ring cycle in 1876.

title: Twilight measures the ozone layer
body: In the 1920s and 30s F. W. Paul Götz found that the ratio of two ultraviolet wavelengths in light from the zenith changes in a telling way as the Sun sets: the Umkehr (“reversal”) effect. Measured through twilight, it reveals how ozone is spread with height, and ground stations still use the method today.

title: The dog watches
body: Ships’ watches traditionally run in four-hour blocks, but the evening one, from 4 to 8 p.m., is split into two ‘dog watches’ of two hours each. That makes an odd number of watches in the day, so the crew’s rota shifts by one each day and nobody stands the same night watch every night. It also lets both watches eat an evening meal.

title: The exposure triangle collapses at civil twilight
body: At civil twilight, a landscape photographer typically needs ISO 400–1600, an f/2.8–4 aperture, and shutter speeds of 1/30 to several seconds. Drop into nautical twilight and long exposures smooth water to glass and turn clouds to streaks. By astronomical twilight’s end, stars trail in exposures over 30 seconds unless you’re tracking. Every stop of light you lose changes everything.

title: Owls hunt by ear, not sight
body: Though owls are icons of the night, the great horned owl begins hunting at dusk — not because it sees well in dim light (though it does), but because it uses precise binaural hearing to locate prey. The asymmetric ear placement in some species like the barn owl gives them 3D sound localisation accurate enough to catch mice in complete darkness. Twilight is just when the hunting begins.

title: A Venus day is longer than its year
body: Venus turns once on its axis every 243 Earth days, slower than it goes round the Sun in 225, and it spins backwards. Put together, one Venus day from sunrise to sunrise lasts about 117 Earth days — and the Sun rises in the west. Under its thick clouds, that long evening would be a slow orange dimming lasting weeks.

title: Clouds lit from below
body: The best sunset colour often comes a few minutes after the Sun has gone. With the Sun just below the horizon, its reddened light passes underneath the clouds and lights their bases, while the ground below is already in shadow. High clouds catch this light longest, glowing after lower ones have turned grey.

title: The Japanese concept of tasogare
body: In Japanese, tasogare (誰そ彼) means dusk or twilight, but its ancient etymology is ‘who is that person?’ — the question you ask when the light is too dim to recognise someone’s face. Like the French ‘entre chien et loup,’ it names dusk as a moment of uncertain identity, the threshold where familiar faces blur into strangers.

title: Wind often dies at sunset
body: Daytime heating drives convection — warm air rising, cool air rushing in. As the sun sets and the ground cools, convection slows and the surface wind that depended on it dies away. Sailors know this as the ‘evening calm,’ a brief window after sunset when the sea flattens and the rigging goes quiet. In coastal areas, the thermal sea breeze that blew all afternoon often reverses as a light land breeze at dusk.

title: Lighthouses kept sunset-to-sunrise hours
body: Lighthouse keepers were typically required to light the lamp at sunset and keep it burning until sunrise, trimming wicks through the night. Modern automated lights switch themselves on with light sensors as the daylight fades in twilight, and off again in the morning.

title: The iridescent cloud lives at twilight
body: Iridescent clouds — patches of brilliant colour in mid-level or high clouds near the sun — are caused by diffraction of sunlight by water droplets or ice crystals of uniform size. They’re most vivid just after sunrise or before sunset, when the sun is low and you can look close to it without being blinded. The colours ripple and shift as the droplets slowly change position.

title: Colour drains before shapes do
body: As twilight deepens you lose colour before you lose detail. The colour-sensing cones stop working first, and the more sensitive but colour-blind rods take over. There is a stretch of dusk when you can still recognise a face but can’t say what colour a shirt is: the world is visible but drained.

title: Great comets of the twilight
body: A comet is often brightest when it swings close to the Sun, which also means it sits low in bright twilight. Comet Ikeya–Seki in 1965 was bright enough to be seen in daylight next to the Sun, and Comet McNaught in 2007 was seen in daylight too, then trailed a huge curved tail across southern evening skies after sunset.

title: The terminator and the space station
body: The line between day and night, the terminator, sweeps across the equator at about 1,670 km/h, the speed of Earth’s turning. The ISS travels about 27,600 km/h and crosses it roughly every 45 minutes. In some seasons, though, its orbit lines up with the terminator and the station stays in sunlight for days at a time.

title: The sundowner
body: A “sundowner” is a drink taken at sunset, a custom that grew up among the British in East Africa and India and lives on in safari camps, where the day’s drive stops at a viewpoint to watch the Sun go down and the night sounds begin.

title: The Moon and planets flash green too
body: The green flash is not only a sunset trick. The same bending and separating of light by the atmosphere can tip the edge of the setting Moon green, and observers have seen Venus and Jupiter flicker green and red as they sink into the horizon haze.

title: The twilight wedge
body: Stand facing away from the sunset and the eastern horizon shows two layers: a dark blue-grey band at the bottom and a pink band above it. Together they are called the twilight wedge. The dark part is Earth’s shadow; the pink is the Belt of Venus. The wedge rises and fades as the Sun sinks.

title: Why dusk skies turn orange, not just red
body: Near sunset, sunlight crosses up to about 40 times more air than at noon. Blue light is scattered out along the way, then green, leaving orange and red. How far the colour goes depends on the air: clean air gives yellows and soft oranges, while dust and haze push it deeper.

title: The Sun looks squashed at sunset
body: A setting Sun often looks oval, wider than it is tall. Refraction lifts its lower edge more than its upper edge, because the lower edge shines through denser air close to the horizon. The squeeze can reach a fifth of its height; unusual layers of warm and cold air can add steps and notches to its edges.

title: The Moon illusion
body: A Moon or Sun near the horizon looks huge, but measure it and it is the same size as when it is high — slightly smaller, in fact, for the Moon. The effect is in your brain, not the sky. No explanation of it is universally accepted, though most involve how we judge distance against the landscape.

title: Novaya Zemlya: the Sun that rose early
body: In 1597 Willem Barentsz’s stranded crew on Novaya Zemlya saw the Sun return two weeks before it should have after the polar night. Extreme refraction through layers of very cold air had bent its light around the curve of the Earth. The Novaya Zemlya effect is named after them.

title: Mirages at the horizon
body: When a layer of warm air lies over cold water, or cold over warm, the setting Sun can break into stacked slices, grow a mushroom top or seem to set twice. These mirages come from light bending as it passes between air layers of different temperature, and they are most common over the sea.

title: Why the dusk sky is blue even with the Sun down
body: After sunset the high atmosphere is still in sunlight. It scatters that light down to you, blue most strongly, so the sky overhead stays blue long after the ground is in shadow. The blue gets deeper as the lit layer rises higher and thinner, until astronomical twilight ends.

title: Purple twilight
body: On very clear evenings, about 15 to 40 minutes after sunset, a faint purplish glow can appear above where the Sun went down. It is red light from the Sun still shining on dust high in the stratosphere, mixed with the blue of the sky around it. After big volcanic eruptions it becomes spectacular.

title: Why clouds turn orange after the Sun has set
body: Clouds are high, so the Sun keeps shining on them for a while after it has set for you on the ground. Its light has crossed so much air on the way that it reaches them already orange or red, and the clouds reflect that colour down.

title: Contrails at dusk
body: A jet’s contrail can blaze orange or pink long after sunset because the plane is flying 10 or 11 km up, still in sunlight. At that height the Sun sets several minutes later than it does on the ground below.

title: The Sun’s rays seem to fan out
body: Crepuscular rays look like they spread out from the Sun like a fan, but they are actually parallel. The spreading is perspective, the same effect that makes straight railway lines seem to meet in the distance.

title: Sunset in a raindrop
body: A rainbow always sits opposite the Sun, centred on the point exactly behind your head. When the Sun is low, that point is only just below the horizon, so evening rainbows are the tallest, nearly a half circle — and often glow red, because the sunlight feeding them has already lost its blue.

title: Red rainbows at sunset
body: Sometimes a rainbow near sunset shows almost only red. The sunlight has crossed so much air that the other colours are scattered away before it reaches the raindrops, leaving little but red to bend into the bow. These red rainbows last only a few minutes.

title: Sun dogs
body: Bright patches of light sometimes appear about 22° either side of a low Sun, at the same height — sun dogs, or parhelia. Flat, hexagonal ice crystals drifting horizontally in high cloud act like tiny prisms. They are most common when the Sun is low, in the morning and evening.

title: The twinkling of the evening star
body: Venus can seem to flash red and green when it is very low in the twilight. It is not the planet changing colour: the thick, turbulent air near the horizon splits its light into colours and throws them about, strongly enough that people have mistaken it for an aircraft.

title: Blue hour’s blue comes from ozone
body: Without ozone, the sky overhead at dusk would look greyish rather than deep blue. The long, slanting path of twilight light passes through a lot of ozone, which absorbs orange and yellow light, leaving the deep blue of the blue hour.

title: The Earth’s shadow on the Moon
body: During a total lunar eclipse the Moon turns coppery red. It sits in Earth’s shadow, lit only by sunlight that has passed through our atmosphere around the edge of the planet — in effect, by every sunrise and sunset on Earth at that moment.

title: Airglow: the sky’s own light
body: Even on the darkest night, the sky is never fully black. High in the atmosphere, atoms and molecules excited by sunlight during the day slowly give off light at night — airglow. It is faint, but it is why a truly dark site still has a faint natural sky glow.

title: Aurorae and twilight
body: At high latitudes the aurora often first appears in the deep twilight, as a pale arc low in the north (or south) that slowly brightens as the sky darkens. In summer the long twilight hides it completely, which is why aurora season runs roughly from late August to April.

title: Noctilucent clouds need the Sun low
body: Noctilucent clouds can only be seen when the Sun is between about 6° and 16° below the horizon: dark enough for the sky, but still shining on the ice 80 km up. That window only opens at latitudes of about 50° to 65° in the weeks around midsummer.

title: Anticrepuscular rays
body: Sometimes the shadows of clouds or mountains at sunset streak across the whole sky and appear to converge again on the opposite horizon, at the point exactly opposite the Sun. These anticrepuscular rays are parallel beams seen in perspective, like rails meeting at both ends of the view.

title: The glory around a plane’s shadow
body: Look down from an aircraft at a cloud layer when the Sun is behind you and you may see the plane’s shadow ringed by small, coloured circles: a glory. It is made by light scattered back from tiny, uniform droplets, and it is easiest to see when the Sun is low.

title: Shadow of a mountain at sunset
body: From a summit at sunrise or sunset, the mountain’s shadow stretches out over the land and appears as a sharp triangle in the air, whatever the mountain’s real shape. It is a trick of perspective: the shadow runs off to a vanishing point far away.

title: Mammatus at sunset
body: Pouch-like mammatus clouds hang from the underside of storm anvils. Low sunlight shining across them at dusk picks out every bulge in gold and red, which is why the most dramatic photographs of them are almost always taken at sunset.

title: The belt of Venus has a matching dawn
body: The Belt of Venus appears at dawn too, in the west this time, just before sunrise. The pink band sits above a blue-grey layer of Earth’s shadow that sinks towards the horizon as the Sun rises, the reverse of the evening show.

title: Evening thunderstorms
body: Over land in summer, many thunderstorms build through the afternoon and peak in the early evening, after a day of heating has driven warm, moist air high into the sky. They often die away after dark, when the ground cools and that engine switches off.

title: Dew at dusk
body: On clear evenings, grass can be wet with dew within an hour or two of sunset. The ground and plants radiate heat to the clear sky and cool below the dew point of the air around them, so water condenses on them. Cloud or wind usually prevents it.

title: Why sound carries further at night
body: On calm evenings, voices and distant trains can sound surprisingly close. The ground cools, the air right above it gets colder than the air higher up, and sound waves bend back towards the ground instead of escaping upwards, travelling further than they would in the day.

title: The Sun is white
body: The Sun only looks yellow, orange or red because of our atmosphere. Seen from space it is essentially white. The warm colours of sunset are the colours left over after the air has scattered much of the blue out of the light.

title: The sky can turn green
body: Before some severe thunderstorms the sky takes on an eerie green tint, often late in the day. One explanation is that the tall storm, full of water and ice, scatters blue light while the low evening sun adds red and yellow, and the mix looks green.

title: Venus can cast a shadow
body: At its brightest, Venus is bright enough to cast faint shadows on a dark, moonless night far from city lights. You need a pale surface and dark-adapted eyes, but people have seen it. Only the Sun and Moon do this more easily.

title: Venus in daylight
body: When Venus is at its brightest and you know exactly where to look, it can be seen in a clear blue daytime sky with the naked eye. The trick is to find it in twilight and keep watching as the sky brightens, or use the Moon as a guide when they are close.

title: Why Venus is never out at midnight
body: Venus orbits inside Earth’s orbit, so from here it never appears more than about 47° from the Sun. That keeps it in the evening or morning sky, setting a few hours after the Sun at most, never high in the sky at midnight.

title: Mercury’s short twilight visits
body: Mercury never strays more than about 28° from the Sun, so it is only ever seen low in bright twilight. The best chances come a few times a year, when it is at its greatest distance from the Sun and the path of the planets stands steeply to the horizon.

title: Mars at opposition
body: Every 26 months or so, Mars comes opposite the Sun in our sky. It rises at sunset, is up all night and shines a fiery orange-red, far brighter than usual. Its ruddy colour comes from iron oxide — rust — in its dust.

title: Jupiter’s moons in twilight
body: Steady binoculars show up to four tiny points in a line beside Jupiter: its largest moons, first seen by Galileo in 1610. They move visibly from night to night, and they are often easiest to spot in twilight, when the sky is dark enough but Jupiter’s glare isn’t overwhelming.

title: Saturn is the faintest bright planet
body: Saturn is the farthest planet you can easily see with the naked eye. It shines with a steady, pale gold light, fainter than Venus, Jupiter or Mars at their best, and it moves so slowly against the stars that it takes about 29.5 years to go once round the sky.

title: Planets don’t twinkle much
body: A quick way to tell a planet from a star in twilight: stars twinkle, planets mostly shine steadily. A planet shows a tiny disc rather than a point, so the air’s turbulence averages out across it. Near the horizon, though, even planets can shimmer.

title: Uranus is just visible to the naked eye
body: Uranus is at the limit of what the naked eye can see from a truly dark site. It was probably seen many times before William Herschel recognised it as a planet in 1781, the first planet discovered in recorded history.

title: The young Moon at dusk
body: A crescent Moon seen after sunset is a waxing, young Moon, a few days after new moon. It always sits low in the west in evening twilight, lit on the side facing the set Sun. Old crescents rise before dawn in the east instead, lit on the other side.

title: Spotting the thinnest crescent
body: Seeing the first thin crescent after new moon in evening twilight is a challenge observers take seriously. Record naked-eye sightings come when the Moon is less than about 16 hours past new. Many calendars, including the Islamic calendar, begin their months with this sighting.

title: Why the Moon rises later each night
body: The Moon moves eastward around the sky by about 13° a day, so it rises on average about 50 minutes later each night. That is why the full Moon rises around sunset, and a week later the Moon doesn’t rise until around midnight.

title: The harvest Moon
body: Around the September equinox, the full Moon near the northern autumn equinox rises only about 20 to 30 minutes later on successive evenings at mid-northern latitudes, instead of the usual 50. Several bright moonrises in a row come soon after sunset, which gave farmers extra light for the harvest.

title: The Moon’s crescent points away from the Sun
body: The horns of a crescent Moon always point away from the Sun. After sunset the lit edge faces down towards where the Sun set, and the tips point up and back. Draw a line across the tips and its perpendicular points roughly to the Sun below the horizon.

title: Earthshine is brightest in spring
body: Earthshine on the dark part of the Moon varies with what the Earth is showing it. It is brightest when lots of cloud and snow face the Moon, since they reflect more sunlight. Measuring earthshine is used to track changes in how much sunlight Earth reflects.

title: The first star you see is usually a planet
body: The first point of light to pop out after sunset is very often not a star but a planet — usually Venus or Jupiter, sometimes Mars or Saturn. They outshine all but the brightest stars, so they appear first in the fading sky.

title: Sirius, the brightest star
body: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, about twice as bright as the next brightest, Canopus. When it is low in the twilight it flashes rapidly in colours, because its light passes through a long path of turbulent air.

title: Why star colours show better in twilight
body: Colour in stars is subtle. Betelgeuse is orange-red, Rigel and Vega blue-white, Arcturus and Aldebaran orange. Many observers find these colours easier to see in the deep blue of late twilight, when their eyes are still using colour-sensitive cones.

title: Polaris barely moves
body: Polaris sits less than a degree from the north celestial pole, so while every other star circles around it through the night, it stays almost fixed. Its height above the northern horizon is roughly your latitude, which is why navigators have used it for centuries.

title: The Summer Triangle rules summer dusks
body: On northern summer evenings, three bright stars — Vega, Deneb and Altair — form a large triangle high in the sky as twilight deepens. They belong to three different constellations: Lyra, Cygnus and Aquila.

title: Orion leaves the evening sky in spring
body: Orion is the classic winter constellation, but by late April it sits low in the west at dusk and soon vanishes into the evening twilight for a few months. It returns in the east before dawn in late summer, a sign in many cultures that autumn is on its way.

title: Satellites flash at dusk
body: In the first hour or two after sunset you can often see satellites crossing the sky as steady moving points. You are in darkness, but they are high enough to still be in sunlight. Later in the night they pass into Earth’s shadow and vanish.

title: The ISS is easiest to see in twilight
body: The International Space Station is best seen shortly after sunset or before sunrise, when it passes overhead while still in sunlight and you are in the dark. It looks like a very bright, steady star crossing the sky in a few minutes, often fading out as it enters Earth’s shadow.

title: Satellite trains
body: Soon after launch, a batch of small satellites can be seen moving in a line like a string of beads across the twilight sky. As they climb to their final orbits and spread out, the train breaks up and they become much fainter.

title: Why stars appear in a set order at dusk
body: As twilight deepens, stars appear in order of brightness: the planets and first-magnitude stars first, then the second-magnitude stars that trace the main shapes of constellations, and finally the faint stars that fill them in only once astronomical twilight is over.

title: Twilight can hide a supernova
body: Supernova 1987A exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud and was spotted in 1987 from Chile. Some bright novae and comets have been found by observers checking low twilight skies, where objects near the Sun turn up before they are lost in its glare.

title: Dark adaptation takes time
body: Your eyes need about 20 to 30 minutes in real darkness to reach their full night sensitivity, and a single glance at a bright light can undo much of it. Observers use dim red lights, which disturb the dark-adapted rods much less.

title: Seeing is best after sunset
body: Just after sunset, the ground and the air above it often settle and the view through a telescope can be unusually steady for a while. Planetary observers make use of these calm moments before the night’s cooling currents set in.

title: Why navigators shoot stars at twilight
body: A sextant needs two things at once: a star to measure and a horizon to measure it from. In full daylight the stars are hidden; in full night the sea horizon disappears. Nautical twilight is the short window when both are visible, which is why sights were traditionally taken at dawn and dusk.

title: Morning stars are harder
body: At dusk the navigator knows where the stars will appear and waits for them. At dawn they must be found first, while it is still too dark to see the horizon well, and then measured quickly before they fade. Many navigators preferred evening sights for exactly this reason.

title: Latitude from Polaris
body: Polaris sits less than a degree from the north celestial pole, so its height above the horizon is very nearly your latitude. Sailors measured it at twilight, when the horizon was still visible, and applied a small correction from a table to allow for the star’s little circle around the pole.

title: Noon sight, the daily anchor
body: Before GPS, the one sight a ship’s navigator almost never missed was local noon, when the Sun reaches its highest point. Its height gave latitude directly. Twilight star sights filled in the rest of the day’s position.

title: The chronometer made longitude possible
body: Finding longitude from the sky needs the exact time at a reference place. John Harrison’s marine timekeepers of the 1700s kept time well enough at sea to make that practical. A clock error of four seconds shifts your longitude by one minute of arc, about one nautical mile at the equator.

title: The Nautical Almanac
body: Published every year, the Nautical Almanac lists where the Sun, Moon, planets and 57 selected navigational stars will be at every hour. It also gives the times of sunrise, sunset, and civil and nautical twilight for a range of latitudes, so a navigator knows when to be on deck with a sextant.

title: The 57 navigational stars
body: The Nautical Almanac’s 57 navigational stars were chosen to be bright, easy to identify and spread across the whole sky, so that at twilight, wherever you are, several good ones are available. Polaris is listed separately, with its own tables.

title: Why a nautical mile is what it is
body: A nautical mile was defined as one minute of arc of latitude, which is why celestial navigation and sea charts fit so well together: one minute of error in a sextant sight is a mile of error in position. Today it is fixed at exactly 1,852 metres.

title: Bird navigators use the sunset
body: Many migratory songbirds set off shortly after sunset. Experiments suggest they use the setting Sun’s position and the pattern of polarised light in the dusk sky to calibrate their magnetic compass before flying through the night.

title: Dung beetles steer by the Milky Way
body: Experiments in South Africa, some run in a planetarium, showed that dung beetles roll their balls in straight lines on clear, moonless nights by using the band of the Milky Way. On overcast nights they wander. They were the first animals shown to use the Milky Way for orientation.

title: Seals may navigate by stars
body: In planetarium experiments, a harbour seal learned to swim toward a chosen star in a projected night sky. That suggests seals could use stars to find their way at sea, though whether wild seals actually do is still unproven.

title: Hours that changed length
body: In ancient Rome and medieval Europe, daylight was divided into twelve hours whatever the season. A summer daytime hour could be well over an hour of our time and a winter one well under. These temporary hours ran from sunrise to sunset, so twilight marked where one set of hours ended and the other began.

title: Italian hours
body: Until Napoleon’s time, much of Italy counted the hours from sunset. The 24th hour struck around dusk, and ‘one o’clock’ was an hour after it. Old clock faces in Italy still show this system, with the hours numbered 1 to 24.

title: Canonical hours and the evening office
body: Monastic prayer followed the light. Vespers was sung at the lighting of the lamps in the evening and Compline before sleep; Lauds greeted the dawn. The word vespers comes from the Latin for evening, and from the evening star.

title: When the Ramadan fast breaks
body: During Ramadan the daily fast runs from dawn to sunset, so the precise moment of sunset is watched closely. In many cities a cannon shot or siren once announced it. The evening meal that breaks the fast is called iftar.

title: The new crescent starts the month
body: The Islamic calendar’s months traditionally begin when the thin new crescent is first seen in the evening twilight. Whether it can be seen depends on how far it is from the Sun and how clear the sky is, so a month can start a day earlier in one country than another.

title: Why Easter moves
body: Easter falls on the Sunday after the first full Moon on or after the spring equinox (using a fixed church date, 21 March, rather than the real one). That is why it can land anywhere from 22 March to 25 April.

title: The Egyptians watched for Sirius at dawn
body: In ancient Egypt, the first sight of Sirius rising in the dawn twilight after months hidden in the Sun’s glare came around the time the Nile began to flood. This ‘heliacal rising’ was an important marker of the year.

title: Heliacal rising
body: A star that has been lost in the Sun’s glare reappears first as a faint point low in the east just before sunrise. That first dawn sighting is its heliacal rising. Ancient calendars across the Mediterranean and Mesopotamia used such sightings to mark the seasons.

title: The Pleiades and the farming year
body: The Greek poet Hesiod told farmers to start the harvest when the Pleiades rise at dawn and to plough when they set at dawn. Their dawn and dusk appearances set the working year for many peoples, from Greece to the Pacific.

title: Matariki
body: In Aotearoa New Zealand, the Māori New Year is marked by the reappearance of the Matariki star cluster (the Pleiades) in the dawn sky in midwinter, around late June or July. Since 2022 it has been a national public holiday.

title: The dog days
body: The ‘dog days’ of summer were named after Sirius, the Dog Star. In ancient Greece and Rome, the hottest weeks came around the time Sirius rose with the Sun at dawn, and people blamed the star for the heat.

title: Why the earliest sunset isn’t on the shortest day
body: In the Northern Hemisphere the earliest sunset comes in early December and the latest sunrise in early January, although the shortest day is around 21 December. The Sun’s noon drifts later through that period because of Earth’s tilt and its elliptical orbit.

title: The equation of time
body: Sundial time and clock time can differ by up to about 16 minutes, depending on the date. This difference, the equation of time, comes from Earth’s tilted axis and its elliptical orbit. It is why sunrise and sunset are not symmetric around noon on your watch.

title: Daylight saving moves sunsets, not daylight
body: Daylight saving time does not add light; it moves the clock so that sunset comes an hour later by the clock. Its supporters wanted to use the evening light; the cost is darker mornings.

title: Time zones stretch the evening
body: Places at the western edge of a time zone see sunset much later by the clock than places at its eastern edge. In China, which uses one time zone across about 60° of longitude, the Sun can set after 10 p.m. by the clock in the far west in summer.

title: Railways killed local time
body: Before the 1800s, every town kept its own time by the Sun, so noon, and every sunset, came a few minutes earlier to the east. Railway timetables made that unworkable. Britain adopted railway time in the 1840s, and in the US the railways introduced standard time zones in 1883.

title: Sunset guns and curfews
body: Many harbours and garrisons fired a gun at sunset. The word curfew is thought to come from the Old French covre-feu, ‘cover fire’: the evening bell that told people to bank their hearths for the night.

title: Midsummer nights that never get dark
body: Anywhere north of about 48.5°N (or south of 48.5°S), the Sun never goes 18° below the horizon on the nights around the summer solstice. Astronomical twilight lasts from sunset to sunrise, and there is no true night at all. That includes Paris, Munich, Seattle and London.

title: Where civil twilight lasts all night
body: North of about 60.5°N, around midsummer, the Sun never sinks more than 6° below the horizon. The whole night is civil twilight: bright enough to read outdoors. Helsinki, Oslo, St. Petersburg and Anchorage all come close to or reach this.

title: The Arctic Circle and the midnight Sun
body: At the Arctic Circle, about 66.5°N, the Sun stays above the horizon for at least one full day around the June solstice. Refraction lifts it enough that the midnight Sun can actually be seen a little way south of the circle too.

title: Polar night is not totally dark
body: Inside the Arctic Circle there are weeks in winter when the Sun never rises. But near the edge of that zone, a few hours of twilight still brighten the middle of the day. Tromsø, Norway, has no sunrise from late November to mid-January, yet enjoys a blue-lit noon.

title: The poles get one long twilight
body: At the North Pole the Sun sets once a year, around the September equinox, and rises around the March equinox. The twilight after sunset lasts for weeks: civil twilight alone lasts roughly two weeks, and full night does not arrive until mid-November.

title: Twilight in the tropics is brief
body: In Singapore, near the equator, astronomical twilight lasts about 70 minutes all year, and civil twilight just over 20. Visitors from higher latitudes often notice that night seems to fall suddenly.

title: Why the equator’s day is always 12 hours
body: At the equator, sunrise and sunset are about 12 hours apart all year. The small extra over 12 hours comes from refraction and the Sun’s size, which add a few minutes to daylight and take them from the night.

title: Equinox days are not exactly equal
body: On the equinox, day and night are not quite equal. Because refraction lifts the Sun and sunrise and sunset are counted from its top edge, daylight is several minutes longer than 12 hours. The date of equal day and night, sometimes called the equilux, falls a few days away from the equinox.

title: Altitude speeds the sunrise
body: From a mountaintop or airliner you can see over the curve of the Earth, so the Sun rises earlier and sets later than for someone at sea level. From 10 km up, sunset can come around 15 minutes later than on the ground below, depending on latitude and season.

title: Chasing the sunset in a plane
body: At the equator, the Earth’s surface moves eastward at about 1,670 km/h. A jet flying west at high latitude, where the ground moves much slower, can keep pace with the Sun, and passengers can watch a sunset that seems to last for hours.

title: Tall buildings get two sunsets
body: In Dubai, residents of the Burj Khalifa’s upper floors see the Sun set a couple of minutes later than people on the ground. Religious authorities there have advised those on high floors to break the Ramadan fast a little later.

title: Watch the sunset twice
body: Lie down on a beach and watch the Sun set. As soon as it disappears, stand up quickly. Your eyes are now higher, can see a little further over the Earth’s curve, and the Sun reappears for a few seconds.

title: Solstice means the Sun stands still
body: Around the solstices, the point where the Sun rises moves along the horizon so slowly that it seems to stop for several days before turning back. The word solstice comes from the Latin sol (Sun) and sistere (to stand still).

title: Sunsets swing along the horizon
body: At mid-northern latitudes the sunset point moves along the western horizon over the year, reaching its farthest north at the June solstice and its farthest south in December. In New York the two extremes are more than 60° apart.

title: Sunset shifts fastest around the equinoxes
body: Around the March and September equinoxes, the time of sunset changes quickly — by more than a minute a day at New York’s latitude. Around the solstices it hardly moves at all. That is why autumn evenings seem to draw in so suddenly.

title: Manhattanhenge
body: Twice a year, around late May and mid-July, the setting Sun lines up exactly with Manhattan’s east–west street grid. The Sun sets framed by buildings at the end of the streets. The name was coined by astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson.

title: Solar alignments in ancient monuments
body: Many ancient buildings frame a sunrise or sunset. At Newgrange in Ireland, built around 3200 BC, the rising Sun on the winter solstice shines along the passage into the inner chamber for about 17 minutes.

title: Chichén Itzá’s serpent of light
body: Around the spring and autumn equinoxes, the late-afternoon Sun at El Castillo pyramid in Chichén Itzá casts a line of triangles down the edge of the northern staircase. It looks like a serpent’s body joining the stone snake head at the bottom.

title: Earth is closest to the Sun in January
body: Earth’s orbit is slightly elliptical, and our closest approach to the Sun, perihelion, falls in early January. Seasons come from the tilt of Earth’s axis, not from distance, which is why the northern winter happens when the Sun is closest.

title: Southern summers are slightly more intense
body: Because Earth is closest to the Sun in January, the Southern Hemisphere’s summer gets about 7% more sunlight at its peak than the northern summer. The larger southern oceans absorb much of the difference.

title: Equinox sunsets point west
body: On the equinox, the Sun rises very close to due east and sets very close to due west anywhere on Earth. A quick look at the sunset on that day is an easy way to find west on your horizon.

title: The latitude with the brightest summer nights
body: In Iceland’s Reykjavík (64°N), the summer Sun sets for only a few hours near midnight, and the sky never gets beyond civil twilight in mid-June. Street lights are switched off for weeks at a time.

title: Antarctica’s winter twilight
body: At the South Pole, the Sun sets around 22 March and does not rise until around 22 September. Researchers who spend the winter there see weeks of twilight, then a long night lit by aurora, and then weeks of dawn colours before the first sunrise.

title: Crepuscular is a word for animals
body: Animals most active at dawn and dusk are called crepuscular, from the Latin crepusculum, ‘twilight’. Deer, rabbits, many cats, hamsters and some mosquitoes are crepuscular. Being out in the half-light can help an animal avoid both daytime predators and the heat of the day.

title: Why deer cross roads at dusk
body: Deer feed most around dawn and dusk, and in autumn they also move more during the mating season. That combination, plus drivers’ eyes adjusting to fading light, is why collisions with deer peak in twilight hours in October and November in much of North America and Europe.

title: Cats see in the twilight
body: A cat’s eyes have a reflective layer behind the retina, the tapetum lucidum, which gives light a second pass through the light-sensitive cells. That is why cats’ eyes shine in headlights. Cats can see in light several times dimmer than people need.

title: Eyeshine tells you who’s there
body: In a torch beam at night, many animals’ eyes glow because of the reflective tapetum behind the retina. The colour varies by species: often green-gold in cats and dogs, and redder in many others. Humans have no tapetum, so our eyes don’t shine back; the red eye in flash photos is light off the blood vessels at the back of the eye.

title: Hedgehogs wake at dusk
body: European hedgehogs are nocturnal and emerge around dusk to forage for beetles, caterpillars and worms. In a single night one can travel a couple of kilometres through gardens, which is why gaps in fences help them.

title: Badgers leave the sett at sunset
body: European badgers usually emerge from their setts around sunset, a little later in the longest days of summer. Watchers wait quietly downwind; a badger’s hearing and smell are far better than its eyesight.

title: Foxes and the evening
body: Red foxes can be active at any time, but in towns and farmland they are mostly seen around dusk and through the night. Their screams on winter nights are part of the mating season.

title: Moths navigate by the Moon, or try to
body: One long-standing idea is that moths keep a steady course by holding a distant light, like the Moon, at a fixed angle; near a lamp that trick sends them spiralling in. Recent high-speed filming suggests something simpler: moths turn their backs to the brightest light, thinking it is the sky, and near a lamp that tips them into loops.

title: Mosquitoes bite at dusk
body: Many mosquitoes, including those that spread malaria and West Nile virus, are most active from dusk into the night. Day-biting species like Aedes aegypti, which carries dengue, are the exception, and bite most in the hours after dawn and before dusk.

title: The daily migration in the ocean
body: Every evening, as the light fades, huge numbers of small fish, krill and plankton rise from the deep sea to feed near the surface, then sink again at dawn. It is the largest daily movement of animals on Earth, and it is timed by twilight.

title: The deep scattering layer
body: During the Second World War, sonar operators found a ‘false bottom’ in the ocean that rose at dusk and sank at dawn. It turned out to be a dense layer of fish and other animals, following the light as they migrate up and down each day.

title: Swifts sleep on the wing
body: At dusk, common swifts gather in screaming flocks, then climb high into the sky to spend the night flying. Tracking studies have shown that common swifts can stay airborne for ten months at a time, only landing to breed.

title: Starling murmurations peak at sunset
body: In autumn and winter, flocks of starlings sometimes tens of thousands strong swirl over their roost in the half-hour around sunset, then drop into the reeds or trees together. Scientists think the display helps keep predators at bay.

title: Nightjars hunt in twilight
body: Nightjars feed on moths and beetles caught in flight at dusk and dawn. Their wide gape and soft, mottled plumage make them almost invisible on the ground by day. The European nightjar’s churring song can be heard on summer evenings.

title: Woodcock and the sky dance
body: In spring, male American woodcock display at dusk: spiralling up into the sky, twittering, then zigzagging back down to the same spot. The performance happens in a narrow window of twilight light levels, and moves later as the evenings lengthen.

title: The evening chorus
body: Many birds sing a short, quieter chorus at dusk as well as the dawn chorus. Blackbirds in particular sing late into the evening, and robins often sing after dark near street lamps.

title: Owls’ eyes are built for twilight
body: Owls’ eyes are packed with rod cells, which work in dim light but see little colour. Their eyes are so large that they cannot move in their sockets, so an owl turns its whole head — up to about 270°.

title: The dawn chorus begins in darkness
body: The dawn chorus often starts before first light. Species with larger eyes, like robins and blackbirds, tend to start earlier, while smaller-eyed birds join later as the light grows.

title: Birds migrate at night
body: Most small songbirds migrate at night. The air is cooler and calmer, fewer predators hunt, and they can feed during the day. On a clear spring or autumn night, a telescope pointed at the full Moon can show migrating birds crossing its face.

title: Glow-worms light up at dusk
body: The European glow-worm is a beetle. On summer evenings, wingless females climb grass stems and glow green from the tip of their abdomen to attract flying males. The glow is chemical, with almost no heat.

title: Fireflies speak in flashes
body: Each firefly species has its own flash pattern. In some places, like the Great Smoky Mountains in Tennessee, one species synchronises its flashes across whole hillsides in early summer. Some predatory fireflies copy other species’ flashes to lure males in and eat them.

title: Mayflies emerge at dusk
body: Mayflies often hatch in huge numbers on summer evenings. Adult mayflies have no working mouthparts and live from a few hours to a couple of days, mating and laying eggs before they die.

title: Cricket chirps and temperature
body: The rate at which crickets chirp in the evening rises with the temperature. For the snowy tree cricket there is a well-known rule of thumb: count the chirps in 14 seconds, add 40, and you get the temperature in °F.

title: Bees head home at dusk
body: Honeybees stop foraging as the light fades and are nearly all home by dark. A few tropical bees and wasps, including some sweat bees, have large eyes adapted for flying in twilight or even at night.

title: Evening primrose opens fast enough to watch
body: Evening primrose flowers open around dusk, some so quickly — within a minute or so — that you can watch them unfold. They are pollinated by night-flying moths, which find them by their pale colour and scent.

title: Night-scented flowers
body: Flowers pollinated by moths tend to be pale, open in the evening and release their strongest scent after dark. Night-scented stock, jasmine, honeysuckle and tobacco plants are all at their most fragrant in the twilight.

title: The four o’clock flower
body: Mirabilis jalapa is called the four o’clock flower because its blossoms open in the late afternoon and stay open overnight, closing the next morning. In some countries it is known as the marvel of Peru.

title: Plants sleep
