body: Many plants fold their leaves in the evening and open them again in the morning. The 18th-century scientist Jean-Jacques d’Ortous de Mairan showed in 1729 that a mimosa kept up the rhythm in a dark cupboard: the first evidence of a biological clock.

title: Linnaeus’s flower clock
body: The botanist Carl Linnaeus suggested planting a garden of flowers that open and close at different times of day, so you could read the time from them. He published the idea in 1751. In practice such gardens keep poor time, because flowers open earlier or later with the weather, the season and the latitude.

title: Flowers that bloom for one night
body: Some night-blooming cacti, like queen of the night (Epiphyllum oxypetalum and Selenicereus species), open a large, fragrant white flower in the evening that wilts by morning. People hold parties to watch them open.

title: Coral spawning follows the Moon and sunset
body: On the Great Barrier Reef, many corals release their eggs and sperm together on a few nights after a full Moon in late spring. The timing within the night is set by sunset: spawning usually starts a few hours after dark.

title: Sea breeze reverses at dusk
body: On sunny days, the land warms faster than the sea, and a sea breeze blows onshore. After sunset the land cools faster, and the breeze dies away and often reverses into a gentle land breeze overnight.

title: Your body clock runs a little long
body: Kept away from daylight, most people’s internal clock runs slightly longer than 24 hours. Morning and evening light keep resetting it. Bright light in the evening shifts it later; morning light shifts it earlier.

title: Blue evening light and sleep
body: The eye has special cells, containing a pigment called melanopsin, that respond most to blue light and signal to the body clock. They are the reason bright, blue-rich light late in the evening can delay sleepiness.

title: Sundowning
body: Some people with dementia become more confused, restless or agitated in the late afternoon and evening. It is called sundowning. The causes are not fully understood; tiredness, fading light and a disrupted body clock are thought to play a part.

title: Why you feel sleepy after sunset
body: As evening falls, the brain’s pineal gland starts releasing melatonin, a hormone that helps prepare the body for sleep. Its release is suppressed by light, so dimming the lights in the evening lets it rise earlier.

title: Body temperature is lowest before dawn
body: Your core body temperature follows a daily cycle, lowest in the early morning hours before you wake and highest in the late afternoon or early evening.

title: Faces fade in twilight
body: In dim light the eye switches to rod cells, which are not concentrated in the centre of vision. Fine detail, like reading or recognising faces, becomes hard, and the world starts to look like a pencil sketch.

title: Why white things glow at dusk
body: In the evening, white and pale flowers seem to glow while the rest of the garden is dark. Your eyes are relying on rod cells, which are most sensitive to blue-green light, so pale and bluish surfaces stand out. It’s also why gardeners plant ‘moon gardens’ of white flowers.

title: Night myopia
body: In low light many people become slightly short-sighted. The pupil widens, letting in light from the edge of the lens where focus is less sharp, and the eye tends to focus a little too close when there is little detail to fix on. It is called night myopia.

title: The dark is never truly black
body: Even in complete darkness, the eye sees a faint grey, sometimes speckled with points of light. This is called eigengrau, ‘own grey’, and comes from signals in the retina and brain, not from light.

title: Driving at dusk is hard
body: Road crashes rise in the twilight hours. The eye is adapting from day to night vision, contrasts fall, and the low Sun can be directly in drivers’ eyes at dawn and dusk. Turning headlights on is as much about being seen as seeing.

title: The yawn at dusk
body: People tend to yawn more in the evening before sleep and in the morning after waking. Yawning is contagious, and one theory is that in groups it helped synchronise rest at dusk.

title: Hunger follows the evening
body: Many people feel hungrier in the evening. Studies of the body clock suggest appetite naturally peaks in the evening, independent of when you last ate.

title: Vitamin D needs a high Sun
body: Your skin makes vitamin D using ultraviolet-B light, which reaches the ground mainly when the Sun is high. When the Sun is lower than about 45° or so, much less UVB reaches you. That means early-morning and evening light, and at high latitudes most of the winter, makes little vitamin D.

title: Sunburn at sunset is unlikely
body: UV light is strongly weakened in the long path through the atmosphere when the Sun is low. The UV index drops quickly in the last hour or two before sunset. However, clear sky and water can still reflect enough UV to burn.

title: Moonlight and animal behaviour
body: Many prey animals, like some rodents, forage less on bright moonlit nights, when predators can see them more easily. Some predators, like lions in the Serengeti, hunt less successfully on moonlit nights and more in the dark before moonrise.

title: Dusk is the hunting hour
body: Many predators are most successful at dawn and dusk, when prey are moving between feeding and resting, and the light favours eyes built for dimness. Lions, tigers and wolves all hunt heavily in these twilight hours.

title: Frogs chorus after sunset
body: On spring nights, male frogs and toads call from ponds to attract mates, starting around dusk. In some species the whole pond calls in rhythm, and a single chorus can be heard more than a kilometre away.

title: Flying squirrels glow pink
body: Flying squirrels emerge at dusk to glide between trees and feed. Some species glow pink under ultraviolet light, a discovery made in 2019 by researchers who shone a UV torch at one by chance.

title: Scorpions glow under UV
body: Scorpions glow bright blue-green under ultraviolet light, making them easy to find at night with a UV torch. Why their skin fluoresces is still debated.

title: Crepuscular, from the Latin
body: The Latin word for twilight was crepusculum, probably from creper, ‘dark’ or ‘dim’. It gave English the words crepuscular (of twilight) and crepuscular rays, and gave French its word for twilight, crépuscule.

title: Dusk and dust are not related
body: Dusk comes from Old English dox, ‘dark’ or ‘swarthy’. Despite the look of it, it has no link to dust.

title: Gloaming
body: The gloaming is a Scots and northern English word for evening twilight, from Old English glōmung. It was made popular far beyond Scotland by the 1911 song ‘Roamin’ in the Gloamin’’ by Harry Lauder.

title: Vesper, the evening star
body: Latin vesper and Greek hesperos both meant evening and the evening star, Venus. They gave us vespers, the evening prayer service, and the Hesperides, the nymphs of the evening who guarded golden apples in the far west.

title: The West is named for the evening
body: Words for ‘west’ in many languages come from words for evening or sunset. The Occident comes from the Latin for ‘setting’ (occidens), and the Orient from ‘rising’ (oriens). The Maghreb, the Arabic name for North Africa’s west, means ‘the place of sunset’.

title: Anatolia means sunrise
body: Anatolia, the Asian part of Turkey, takes its name from the Greek anatolē, ‘rising’ or ‘east’ — the land of the sunrise as seen from Greece. The Levant comes from the French for ‘rising’, for the same reason.

title: Japan, the land of the rising Sun
body: The name Japan, Nihon or Nippon in Japanese, is written with characters meaning ‘origin of the Sun’. From China, Japan lay toward the sunrise.

title: Magic hour
body: Filmmakers call the time around sunset (and sunrise) ‘magic hour’ or ‘golden hour’, when light is soft, warm and flattering. Terrence Malick shot much of Days of Heaven (1978) in these short windows each day.

title: Dawn and day share a root
body: The English word dawn comes from the old verb dawen, ‘to become day’. It shares its root with day itself. In many languages, words for dawn and morning also give words for tomorrow, as in German Morgen and Spanish mañana.

title: Night and the Indo-European root
body: The word night has close relatives across the Indo-European languages: German Nacht, Latin nox, Greek nyx, Sanskrit nakt-. All go back to Proto-Indo-European, spoken perhaps 5,000 or more years ago.

title: Macbeth’s thickening light
body: Shakespeare’s plays are full of twilight. In Macbeth, ‘Light thickens, and the crow / Makes wing to the rooky wood’ marks dusk as the time for dark deeds, just before Banquo is murdered.

title: Gray’s Elegy begins at dusk
body: Thomas Gray’s ‘Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard’ (1751) opens: ‘The curfew tolls the knell of parting day’. The whole poem is set in the fading light as the ploughman heads home.

title: Tennyson’s ‘Crossing the Bar’
body: Tennyson’s short poem ‘Crossing the Bar’ (1889) begins ‘Sunset and evening star’ and uses twilight and the evening bell as images of a peaceful death. He asked that it be printed at the end of every collection of his poems.

title: T.S. Eliot’s evening
body: T.S. Eliot’s ‘The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock’ (1915) opens with one of the most famous images of dusk in modern poetry: ‘When the evening is spread out against the sky / Like a patient etherised upon a table’.

title: The Owl of Minerva flies at dusk
body: The philosopher Hegel wrote in 1820 that ‘the owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of the dusk’, meaning that we understand an era only as it ends. Minerva, goddess of wisdom, was said to have the owl as her bird.

title: Dylan Thomas and the dying light
body: Dylan Thomas’s poem ‘Do not go gentle into that good night’ (1951), written to his dying father, repeats the line ‘Rage, rage against the dying of the light’. Twilight is its image for the end of life.

title: The Celtic Twilight
body: W. B. Yeats published a book of Irish folklore called The Celtic Twilight in 1893. The title came to stand for the whole late-19th-century revival of Irish myth and literature.

title: Monet’s Houses of Parliament
body: Claude Monet painted London’s Houses of Parliament again and again between 1900 and 1905, many of them at sunset through the coal smoke and fog over the Thames. The pollution turned the light purple, orange and gold.

title: Impression, Sunrise gave Impressionism its name
body: Claude Monet’s 1872 painting of the harbour at Le Havre at dawn, ‘Impression, Sunrise’, gave the Impressionist movement its name, after a critic used it mockingly in 1874.

title: Van Gogh’s starry skies
body: Van Gogh’s ‘Café Terrace at Night’ (1888) was one of his first paintings with a starry sky, painted on the spot in Arles. He wrote to his sister that the night is ‘much more alive and richly coloured than the day’.

title: Friedrich’s watchers at dusk
body: Caspar David Friedrich, the German Romantic painter, often painted people seen from behind watching the sky at dawn, dusk or moonrise, as in ‘Two Men Contemplating the Moon’ (around 1819–20).

title: Whistler’s nocturnes
body: James McNeill Whistler named his paintings of the Thames at dusk and night ‘Nocturnes’, borrowing the word from music. The critic John Ruskin attacked one in 1877, Whistler sued him for libel, and won a farthing in damages.

title: Hopper’s evening light
body: Edward Hopper often painted American towns in late light, as in ‘Nighthawks’ (1942). In it, the harsh light of a diner spills out onto a dark street corner — an artificial twilight.

title: Magritte’s day and night
body: René Magritte’s ‘The Empire of Light’ series shows a street at night under a bright daytime sky. He painted it again and again, in oils and gouache, from the late 1940s into the 1960s.

title: Nocturnes
body: A nocturne is a piece inspired by the night. The Irish composer John Field invented the piano nocturne in the early 1800s, and Chopin wrote 21 of them.

title: Clair de Lune
body: Debussy’s ‘Clair de Lune’ (moonlight), from his Suite bergamasque, takes its title from a poem by Paul Verlaine. It is one of the most recognised pieces of classical music ever written.

title: Serenades were evening songs
body: A serenade was originally music performed in the evening, often under a window. The word comes from Italian sereno, ‘calm, clear sky’, though it became linked with sera, ‘evening’.

title: Dawn in the Grand Canyon
body: Ferde Grofé’s ‘Grand Canyon Suite’ (1931) begins with ‘Sunrise’ and includes ‘Sunset’, painting the changing light on the canyon walls in music.

title: Beethoven’s ‘Moonlight’ was not his title
body: Beethoven called his Piano Sonata No. 14 a ‘fantasy-like sonata’. The name ‘Moonlight’ came from a critic, Ludwig Rellstab, after Beethoven’s death, who said the first movement reminded him of moonlight on Lake Lucerne.

title: Diwali lights the new Moon
body: Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, is celebrated on the darkest night of the lunar month Kartika, the new Moon, usually in October or November. Lamps are lit at dusk to welcome prosperity and mark the victory of light over darkness.

title: Hanukkah candles are lit at nightfall
body: During Hanukkah, candles are lit each evening after sunset for eight nights. Tradition says they should burn for at least half an hour after the stars come out.

title: Mid-autumn Moon
body: The Mid-Autumn Festival in China and East Asia falls on the full Moon of the eighth lunar month, near the September equinox. Families gather in the evening to watch the Moon rise and eat mooncakes.

title: Midsummer bonfires
body: In Scandinavia, the Baltic states and Finland, midsummer is celebrated on the lightest night of the year with bonfires, dancing and flower crowns, around 23–24 June. In Finland it is called Juhannus, and in Sweden Midsommar.

title: Evening passeggiata
body: In Italian towns, many people take a slow walk through the streets and squares in the early evening, the passeggiata. In Spain, a similar evening stroll is the paseo.

title: Spain’s late dinner
body: In Spain, dinner is often eaten after 9 p.m. One reason is the clock: Spain uses Central European Time, though it lies mostly west of Greenwich, so its sunsets come late by the clock.

title: Evensong
body: Evensong is the evening prayer service of the Church of England, traditionally sung around sunset. Choral evensong is still sung daily in many English cathedrals.

title: Hawaiian chant at sunrise
body: In Hawaiian tradition, ‘E Ala E’ is a chant greeting the sunrise. It is performed at dawn to welcome the Sun and the new day.

title: Tyndall’s blue sky in a tube
body: In the 1860s John Tyndall shone light through a tube of fine particles and saw it scatter blue from the side and redden straight through. It was an early lab model of why the sky is blue and sunsets red.

title: Rayleigh named the scattering
body: Lord Rayleigh showed in 1871 that very small particles scatter short wavelengths much more strongly than long ones — roughly five to ten times more for blue and violet than for red. The scattering that colours the sky and the sunset now carries his name.

title: Einstein and the blue sky
body: In 1910 Einstein showed that the blue of the sky comes from small, random fluctuations in the density of the air itself, not from dust or water. It was a key step in understanding Rayleigh scattering in a gas.

title: Sunsets defeated early cameras
body: Early photographic plates were slow and far more sensitive to blue than red, so sunsets were among the hardest subjects. Colour photographs of sunsets only became common after colour film spread in the mid-20th century.

title: Blackout Britain
body: During the Second World War, Britain was blacked out every night from sunset to sunrise to hide towns from bombers. Daily newspapers printed the blackout times, and ARP wardens enforced them.

title: Double summer time
body: During the Second World War, Britain adopted ‘double summer time’, two hours ahead of Greenwich Mean Time in summer. It pushed sunset in London past 10 p.m. around midsummer, giving extra evening light for farm and factory work.

title: Twilight on the Moon’s horizon glow
body: Astronauts on the Apollo missions and the Surveyor landers saw a faint glow along the Moon’s horizon after sunset. It is thought to be sunlight scattered by fine dust lifted above the surface.

title: Titan’s hazy twilight
body: Saturn’s moon Titan has a thick, hazy atmosphere. The Cassini spacecraft saw its haze light up around its edge like a ring of twilight, and it is thick enough that sunlight reaches the surface as a dim orange glow.

title: Pluto has blue haze
body: When New Horizons flew past Pluto in 2015, it looked back toward the Sun and saw blue haze layers glowing in Pluto’s thin atmosphere, lit from behind like a twilight halo.

title: Sunsets on Jupiter would be dim
body: Jupiter is five times further from the Sun than Earth, so sunlight there is about 1/27th as bright. The Sun would look about a fifth as wide as from Earth, still dazzling, but its twilight would be faint.

title: Uranus has 42-year days
body: Uranus is tipped on its side, so each pole spends about 42 Earth years in continuous sunlight, then 42 in darkness. At the poles, sunrise and sunset come once every 42 years.

title: Mercury’s double sunrise
body: On Mercury, the Sun’s apparent motion across the sky can briefly reverse. At some places, the Sun rises, stops, sets again, then rises once more, because Mercury’s orbital speed near perihelion briefly outpaces its slow spin.

title: Sunsets on Titan last hours
body: Titan takes almost 16 Earth days to rotate once with respect to the Sun, so the slow fade from day to night there would take hours, under a dim orange sky.

title: Earth seen from the Moon has phases
body: Seen from the Moon, Earth goes through phases too, opposite to the Moon’s. When the Moon is a thin crescent from Earth, an astronaut on the Moon’s near side would see a nearly full Earth — which is what lights up earthshine.

title: Exoplanets found by starlight at their twilight
body: When an exoplanet passes in front of its star, some starlight passes through the ring of twilight around the planet’s edge. Telescopes like JWST read the colours of that light to detect gases like carbon dioxide and water in the planet’s atmosphere.

title: Rocket launches at twilight look alien
body: When a rocket launches shortly after sunset or before sunrise, its exhaust plume climbs into sunlight while the ground is dark. The plume glows in bright, spreading colours and is sometimes mistaken for a UFO. Launches from California have caused this ‘twilight phenomenon’ over the southwestern US.

title: Meteors are more common after midnight
body: More meteors are seen in the hours after midnight than in the evening. By then you are on the side of Earth facing forward in its orbit, so Earth runs into more meteoroids, like a car’s windscreen catching more rain than its rear window.

title: Comets have tails that point away from the Sun
body: A comet’s tails point away from the Sun, so a comet in the evening twilight has its head toward the horizon and its tail sweeping up. After passing the Sun, a comet travels tail-first.

title: Hesperus and Phosphorus
body: The ancient Greeks at first thought the evening star, Hesperus, and the morning star, Phosphorus, were two different objects. Both are Venus. The philosopher Gottlob Frege later used the pair to show how two names can mean the same thing yet tell you different things.

title: Selene rises after the Sun sets
body: In Greek myth, Selene, goddess of the Moon, drove her chariot across the night sky after her brother Helios had finished his daytime journey. Their sister Eos, the dawn, went ahead of Helios each morning.

title: Ushas, the Vedic dawn
body: In the Rigveda, the oldest of the Hindu scriptures, the dawn goddess Ushas is praised in around twenty hymns. She drives away the darkness and wakes every living thing each morning.

title: Nyx, older than the gods
body: In Greek myth Nyx, the Night, was one of the first beings to emerge from Chaos. Even Zeus was said to fear her. Her children included Hypnos (Sleep), Thanatos (Death) and Hemera (Day).

title: Aurora’s name lives on
body: Aurora was the Roman goddess of the dawn. Galileo is often credited with naming the northern lights aurora borealis, the ‘northern dawn’, because they can look like a sunrise glow on the northern horizon.

title: Red sky in the Bible
body: The weather saying about a red sky is very old. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says: ‘When it is evening, ye say, It will be fair weather: for the sky is red. And in the morning, It will be foul weather to day: for the sky is red and lowring.’

title: Mackerel sky
body: ‘Mackerel sky and mares’ tails make tall ships carry low sails’ is an old sailor’s rhyme. The rippled clouds and wispy streaks, often lit pink at sunset, can come before an approaching warm front and its rain.

title: The witching hour
body: Folklore has long held that witches, ghosts and spirits are most active in the dead of night, often put at midnight or around three in the morning. Dusk, a boundary between day and night, was also thought to be a time when the other world came close.

title: The evening temperature inversion
body: On clear, calm evenings the ground cools quickly by radiating heat to the sky, and the air near it cools with it. The coldest air pools in valleys and hollows, which is why frost forms first in low spots and smoke from chimneys spreads flat instead of rising.

title: Clear skies make cold nights
body: Clouds act like a blanket, sending heat back down to the ground. On a clear night nothing slows the heat escaping to space, so the temperature can drop sharply after sunset — deserts can cool by 20 °C or more in a night.
